title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Forward live MEM load data into EX
motivation:
The in-order pipeline inserts a bubble whenever an instruction immediately
consumes a load result, even though the zero-wait memory model presents that
result combinationally while the load is in MEM. CoreMark's list and matrix
code repeatedly loads a value before using it. Removing these bubbles should
improve iterations per cycle without changing the retirement width.

title: Decouple DIV and REM with an iterative EX unit
motivation:
The bench core puts four full-width combinational divide and remainder operations
on its one-cycle EX datapath. That costs LUTs and can constrain Fmax for every
CoreMark instruction, while the timed matrix, list, and state loop has effectively
no divide traffic. A closely related reference core gained Fmax and shed thousands
of LUTs after moving these operations to a multicycle unit. The bench baseline has
only 437 LUT4s of margin under its 10000-LUT4 target, making this structural change
especially promising.

INT_MIN/-1 behavior. Preserve the RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS result substitutions and
exercise the same launch/complete interlock in formal mode. This should raise
median Fmax with negligible change to CoreMark's marker-to-marker cycle count.

title: Predict control flow with a small branch target buffer
motivation: The current fetch PC advances by four until EX resolves every taken branch or jump. Each taken control transfer flushes the younger instruction, wasting a cycle in a branch-heavy CoreMark loop. A small predictor can remove that bubble on repeated control transfers without changing retirement or the memory interface.

title: Segment the RVFI retirement order counter
motivation:
The bench core increments a 64-bit RVFI order register on every retirement.
That wide carry path is present in the FPGA timing design because the RVFI
signals feed the bench output logic. A related RV32IM core gained 6.34%
fitness from four 16-bit order-counter segments with no cycle-count change.
The bench core still uses the original monolithic incrementer, so this is
a small timing optimization with direct supporting evidence.

title: Move high-half multiply off the single-cycle EX path
motivation:
The divider change raised fitness by removing rarely used wide arithmetic
from the one-cycle EX path. The ALU still builds three full 64-bit products
for MUL, MULH, MULHU, and MULHSU. Those high-half product paths must meet
the clock period even when CoreMark is executing ordinary 32-bit operations.
CoreMark's matrix arithmetic needs the low-half MUL throughput, so that
operation should remain single-cycle.

title: Share the divider comparison and subtraction
motivation:
The iterative divider currently compares a 33-bit trial remainder against
the divisor and separately subtracts the same operands every RUN cycle.
These overlapping carry networks consume LUTs and routing even though
CoreMark rarely divides. The prior RVFI counter segmentation improved
fitness by shortening a timing path without changing the cycle count;
this is another small timing and placement opportunity in the current core.

title: Decouple fetch from issue with a two-entry prefetch queue
motivation:
The current IF stage holds its fetch PC whenever load-use, dmem, or divider
backpressure stops decode. It discards otherwise ready instruction-bus cycles
during those pauses, then pays a fresh imem stall when issue resumes. The
fitness cosim independently rejects about 22% of instruction fetch cycles.
A small elastic queue can use paused issue cycles to fetch ahead without
adding a predictor or lengthening the zero-wait pipeline.

both bus and pipeline stalls. Keep each instruction's PC paired with its
word for RVFI, and retain the nret=1 retirement interface and all existing
trap and memory semantics. This should recover part of the imem-stall cost

The previous 16-entry target buffer reduced CoreMark from 4,491,817 to
4,234,021 timed cycles, but on the iterative-divider core it lowered Fmax
from 156.91 to 142.61 MHz and reduced fitness to 336.82. Direct branch and
JAL targets are encoded in the fetched instruction, so storing 32-bit
targets and comparing tags adds hardware that these transfers do not need.

title: Retire stalled RAM stores through a one-entry slot
motivation:
A store in MEM currently freezes the entire pipeline whenever dmem is not
ready, although its address, data, and byte mask are already known. The
fitness run applies random dmem stalls, so those freezes cost CoreMark

the branch outcome is known, without predicting direction or comparing two

title: Predict backward branches with low-byte PC steering
motivation:
The current core spends 4,491,817 cycles on CoreMark because taken branches
redirect from EX. Predicting short backward branches previously cut this to
4,303,997 cycles, but fetch-side boundary checks and PC selection reduced
Fmax to 171.59 MHz, leaving fitness 2.42% below the current best. A narrower
PC update could retain the cycle gain without putting those checks on the
fetch register's critical path.

title: Move AUIPC selection out of the common ALU input path
motivation:
The EX stage currently selects between the forwarded rs1 value and PC
before every ALU operation, solely to support AUIPC. This 32-bit mux
also precedes common CoreMark arithmetic, address generation, shifts,
and multiplication. Earlier one-hot ALU selection improved routed Fmax,
while adding operation selection ahead of arithmetic has hurt it. The
current core has enough LUT headroom for one separate PC-plus-immediate
adder, and this change should leave CoreMark cycle count unchanged.

title: Pipeline multiplication across EX and MEM
motivation:
The current EX stage must finish three full-width products and select their
results in one clock, even though ordinary CoreMark instructions do not use
the high-half variants. Earlier high-half-only units added an EX interlock
without shortening the common low-half MUL path and lost Fmax. Splitting all
multiplication at the existing EX/MEM boundary targets that path while
allowing independent instructions to keep issuing every cycle.

512-byte block and signed nine-bit displacement, versus 75 that fit the
